summary: Redefines the meaning of the two data link layer codepoints that RFC 3032 set up to tell MPLS unicast from MPLS multicast. The original multicast distinction was never deployed, so both codepoints can now carry multicast packets, and the second keeps its role for upstream-assigned labels. It updates RFC 3032 and RFC 4023.

plainLanguage.summary: MPLS puts labels on packets so routers can forward them without reading the IP header. This RFC sorts out how a router marks a frame that carries such a packet when the packet is going to many destinations. It also fixes the group address that the frame uses, which the earlier specification never defined.

questions: what is the mpls multicast codepoint
subtitle: What the two MPLS ethertypes now mean, and how a multicast MPLS packet is addressed on Ethernet.

tldr.problem: RFC 3032 gave MPLS two ethertypes, one for unicast and one for multicast, but the multicast one was never deployed and the split it described turned out not to be the one operators need.
tldr.mechanism: Both ethertypes can now carry multicast packets. Ethertype 0x8848 is kept for the one case that still needs telling apart: a multicast frame whose top label was assigned upstream rather than by the receiver.
tldr.outcome: The RFC updates RFC 3032 and RFC 4023, and it also specifies the MAC destination address to use for a multicast MPLS packet, which RFC 3032 left open.

today: RFC 5332 is a Proposed Standard on the Internet standards track, and no RFC in the site index obsoletes or updates it. It updates RFC 3032 and RFC 4023, and the RFC notes that the multicast codepoint it redefines was never deployed, so the interoperability problem it describes is not expected in practice.

sections.title: Why the Codepoints Are Redefined
sections.content:
RFC 3031 defines the Next Hop Label Forwarding Entry, the NHLFE. The NHLFE for a particular label maps the label into a next hop, among other things. When an MPLS packet is received, its top label is mapped to an NHLFE, and the packet is sent to the next hop the NHLFE specifies.

This document calls a particular MPLS label a multicast label in a particular context if the NHLFE to which it is mapped specifies a set of next hops, with the semantics that the packet is to be replicated and a copy sent to each of them. The definition accommodates a set with a single member. What makes a label a multicast label in a context is the semantics attached to the set: the intention to replicate the packet and transmit to all members of the set if there is more than one.

RFC 3032 established two data link layer codepoints for MPLS: one to indicate that the frame carries an MPLS unicast packet, and the other to indicate that it carries an MPLS multicast packet. The term multicast packet is not precisely defined in RFC 3032, though one may presume that the multicast codepoint was intended to identify the packet's top label as a multicast label. However, that codepoint was never deployed, and further development of the procedures for MPLS multicast showed that there is a need for two codepoints but that the use of them is not properly captured by RFC 3032.

In particular, there is no need for a codepoint to indicate whether the top MPLS label is a multicast label, because when the receiver looks up the top label, the NHLFE already says whether or not the label is a multicast label. This document therefore updates RFC 3032 and RFC 4023 by re-specifying the use of the codepoints, and the old use of the multicast codepoint is deprecated.

The RFC is explicit about the consequence: an implementation that does MPLS multicast according to RFC 3032 and RFC 4023 will be unable to interoperate with an implementation that does it according to this document. It notes that the deployed platforms that support the deprecated use of the codepoints lack the control plane mechanisms needed for MPLS multicast, and that the absence of that control plane prevents them from trying to interoperate, so the problem is unlikely to arise in practice. The RFC also fills a gap in RFC 3032, which allows an MPLS packet to be carried in an ethernet multicast frame but does not say how the MAC destination address is to be set in that case.
sections.plainLanguage: The original idea was that one Ethernet type number would mean unicast and the other multicast. That was never used in practice, and it turned out to be the wrong split. The new rule keeps two type numbers, but they now tell the receiver something else, and the multicast case does not need a separate number at all.

sections.title: Upstream-Assigned and Downstream-Assigned Labels
sections.content:
Suppose a labelled packet P is sent from Label Switching Router R1 to LSR R2, where R1 puts label L on the packet's label stack and R2 has to look up label L to find the corresponding Forwarding Equivalence Class, F.

If the binding between L and F was made by R2 and advertised to R1, the label binding is downstream-assigned. RFC 3031 only discusses downstream-assigned label bindings. If the binding was made by R1 and advertised to R2, it is upstream-assigned. If the binding was made by a third party, R3, and then advertised to both R1 and R2, it is also referred to as upstream-assigned.

Upstream-assigned labels are not required to come from the same label space as downstream-assigned labels, and the procedures for properly interpreting an upstream-assigned label are given in RFC 5331. When a packet emerges through a tunnel, the downstream LSR must know whether the label now at the top of the stack has an upstream-assigned or a downstream-assigned binding. The ability to use upstream-assigned labels is an OPTIONAL feature, and they MUST NOT be used unless it is known that the downstream LSR supports them. This document makes no changes to the procedures for unicast labels.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally the router that receives a label is the one that chose what it means, and tells the sender. Here the sender may choose instead. When that happens the receiver has to be told, because it interprets the label differently.

sections.title: Point-to-Point, Point-to-Multipoint and Multipoint-to-Multipoint
sections.content:
The RFC distinguishes three kinds of data link or tunnel. A point-to-point link associates two systems, so that what one transmits is received by the other and only the other. For a given direction of a given point-to-point link, either every MPLS packet carries an upstream-assigned label or every packet carries a downstream-assigned label, and in the absence of any other information the use of downstream-assigned labels MUST be presumed by default.

A point-to-multipoint link associates n systems, so that only one of them can transmit onto the link and the transmissions may be received by the other n-1 systems. The top labels of all MPLS packets transmitted on a particular point-to-multipoint link or tunnel MUST be of the same type, so all the receivers on the tunnel must know in advance whether upstream-assigned or downstream-assigned labels are being used in it.

A multipoint-to-multipoint link associates n systems so that any of them can transmit and the transmissions may be received by the others. Three scenarios are possible: it is known that every top label on the link is downstream-assigned, it is known that every top label is upstream-assigned, or some packets have upstream-assigned top labels while others have downstream-assigned ones.

If, and only if, the third scenario applies, the data link or tunnel encapsulation MUST provide a codepoint that says whether the top label of the encapsulated packet is upstream-assigned or downstream-assigned. If a particular type of data link or tunnel provides no such codepoint, then the third scenario MUST NOT be used. The rest of the document specifies the procedures for setting the data link layer codepoints and address fields.
sections.plainLanguage: On a link with only two ends, or where only one end ever sends, the router at the far end can be told once how to read the labels. On a shared link where any end may send, the label type can differ from packet to packet, so the frame itself has to carry that information.

sections.title: The Codepoints for Ethernet, PPP, GRE and IP
sections.content:
Ethernet is an example of a multipoint-to-multipoint data link. Ethertype 0x8847 is used whenever a unicast ethernet frame carries an MPLS packet. It is also used whenever a multicast ethernet frame carries an MPLS packet, except where the top label of the packet has an upstream-assigned binding. Ethertype 0x8848, formerly known as the MPLS multicast codepoint, is to be used only when an MPLS packet whose top label is upstream-assigned is carried in a multicast ethernet frame.

PPP is an example of a point-to-point data link. When a PPP frame carries an MPLS packet, the PPP Protocol field is always set to 0x0281.

For Generic Routing Encapsulation, RFC 4023 is modified. If the IP destination address of the GRE is a unicast IP address, the ethertype value 0x8847 MUST be used in all cases for the MPLS-in-GRE encapsulation. If the IP destination address is a multicast IP address, the ethertype value 0x8847 MUST be used when the top label of the encapsulated packet is downstream-assigned, and 0x8848 MUST be used when the top label is upstream-assigned. Where it is known, through procedures outside the scope of the specification, that a GRE packet with a multicast destination address has an upstream-assigned top label, the occurrence of the 8847 codepoint in such a packet MUST be considered an error, and the packet MUST be discarded.

RFC 4023 is also modified in the IP protocol number: the IPv4 Protocol Number field or the IPv6 Next Header field is always set to 137, whether or not the encapsulated MPLS packet is an MPLS multicast packet. If the IP destination address of the IP encapsulation is an IP multicast address, the tunnel may be considered a point-to-multipoint or a multipoint-to-multipoint tunnel, and in either case either all the encapsulated MPLS packets in that tunnel have a downstream-assigned label at the top of the stack, or all of them have an upstream-assigned one.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules differ a little for each kind of link. Ethernet and PPP have fixed fields, and the tunnel protocols carry an inner Ethernet type field. Only Ethernet and GRE can signal the upstream-assigned case, and the IP header always uses protocol number 137.

sections.title: The Ethernet MAC Address for Multicast MPLS
sections.content:
When an LSR transmits a multicast MPLS packet in a multicast ethernet frame, it MUST set the MAC Destination Address to the value 01-00-5e-8v-wx-yz, where vwxyz is a 20-bit, five-nibble value set in one of two ways. It MAY be set to 0, or it MAY be set to the value of one of the MPLS labels on the packet's label stack. Which procedure is the default in any particular LSR is implementation-dependent, but LSRs using the two different procedures MUST interoperate: an LSR MUST NOT filter packets for which vwxyz has been set to zero, and it MUST NOT indiscriminately filter all packets for which vwxyz has not been set to zero.

If an LSR sets vwxyz to the value of one of the labels on the label stack, and that stack contains two or more labels, then by default vwxyz MUST be set to the value of the second label on the stack, meaning the label in the stack entry immediately below the topmost one. The LSR MAY be configured to use a different label. If the packet has only one label, the value of that label is used instead of the non-existent second label.

The RFC explains why the second label is the useful one. It is expected that an LSR will push two labels, with the topmost being a context label that is the same for all MPLS packets the LSR transmits onto the ethernet, and the second being different for different LSPs. If the MAC DA value is a function of the second label, more of the LSP-specific information about the packet appears in the MAC DA field, which can be used to filter multicast packets with unexpected non-zero values of vwxyz. The use of ethernet and IP broadcast addresses, as distinct from multicast addresses, is outside the scope of the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: A multicast frame needs a group address. For MPLS the RFC reserves a range of the multicast address space and puts the label into the last part of the address, so a receiver can tell at a glance which stream a frame belongs to. The alternative, an all-zero value, is allowed too, and the two must work side by side.

sections.title: Address Ranges and Ethertype Names
sections.content:
IANA owns the set of ethernet multicast addresses in the range 01-00-5e-00-00-00 to 01-00-5e-ff-ff-ff. Addresses in the range 01-00-5e-00-00-00 to 01-00-5e-7f-ff-ff are already reserved for use when an ethernet multicast frame carries an IP multicast packet.

IANA has reserved ethernet addresses in the range 01-00-5e-80-00-00 to 01-00-5e-8f-ff-ff for use when an ethernet multicast frame carries an MPLS multicast packet. Addresses in this range are valid when used with ethertype 8847 or 8848.

As this document modifies the usage of ethertypes 8847 and 8848, IANA has changed the description of these ethertypes. Ethertype 8847 is defined as MPLS, as defined in RFC 3032 and in this document. Ethertype 8848 is defined as MPLS with upstream-assigned label, as defined in this document.
sections.plainLanguage: A block of the Ethernet multicast address space is set aside for MPLS, above the block already used for IP multicast. The names of the two ethertypes are changed to match what they now mean.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3032 and RFC 4023 apply.

Malicious changing of the codepoint may result in loss or misrouting of packets. However, altering the codepoint without also altering the label does not result in a predictable effect. Malicious alteration of the MAC DA on an ethernet can result in packets being received by a third party rather than by the intended recipient.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC leaves security to the two documents it updates and adds one observation: changing the type field or the group address of a frame can send packets to the wrong place. Changing the type field alone does not do anything predictable, because the labels would no longer match.

items.label: MPLS
items.desc: Unicast frames, and multicast frames whose top label is downstream-assigned.

items.label: MPLS WITH UPSTREAM-ASSIGNED LABEL
items.desc: Only for a multicast frame whose top label is upstream-assigned.

items.label: PPP PROTOCOL FIELD
items.desc: Always used when a PPP frame carries an MPLS packet.

items.label: IP PROTOCOL NUMBER
items.desc: Always used for MPLS in IP, whether the packet is multicast or not.

viz.caption: THE THREE KINDS OF LINK AND TUNNEL

items.title: Point-to-point
items.text: Two systems: what one transmits is received by the other and only the other.

items.title: Point-to-multipoint
items.text: n systems where only one may transmit and the others may receive.

items.title: Multipoint-to-multipoint
items.text: n systems where any of them may transmit and the others may receive.

layers.detail: One or more labels on top of the packet

layers.detail: An ethernet frame, a GRE tunnel or an IP tunnel
